articles.content:
To planlagte konserter i Russland med den amerikanske rapperen Kanye West (Ye) er avlyst, opplyser arrangøren.

Avlysningen kommer under to måneder etter at konsertene i St. Petersburg ble kunngjort. Den opprinnelige konsertarenaen trakk seg kort tid etter at billettsalget startet.

Arrangøren beklager avlysningen og lover refusjon til billettkjøpere. Kanye West har foreløpig ikke kommentert avlysningen.

Ye, som er utestengt fra å opptre i flere europeiske land på grunn av tidligere antisemittiske utsagn, ville vært den største vestlige artisten til å opptre i Russland siden fullskalainvasjonen av Ukraina i 2022.

articles.title: Overqualified and underpaid: The reality facing Norway's foreign workers
articles.content:
Add The Local as a preferred source
    
                        
                                        
                        Four in ten highly educated immigrants in Norway are currently employed in roles below their skill level. This mismatch takes a personal and financial toll on these workers and means Norway misses out on valuable talent.

Relocating to Norway often comes with high expectations, yet for thousands of foreign professionals, arrival marks the beginning of an uphill struggle.

A  very common story in Norway is that even with Master’s degrees and years of experience, many newcomers (or even long time residents) cannot break into their own field.

Given Norway’s high cost of living, immediate income is an absolute necessity. As a result, highly qualified individuals are forced to take up jobs in cleaning, hospitality or retail.

Stories of former lawyers with fifteen years of legal experience cleaning houses or experienced engineers delivering food are far from rare and unfortunately not anecdotal. They reflect an everyday reality for a big portion of Norway’s international workforce.

A study from Statistics Norway (SSB) shows that these personal stories are part of a bigger ongoing structural problem.

Data shows that in 2025, 93,000 immigrants with higher education in Norway worked in jobs that did not match their qualifications. This made up 40 percent of all foreign workers with higher education degrees.

This means many immigrants are employed in roles with lower educational requirements that are completely unrelated to the fields they spent years studying and specialising in.

The highest rate of overqualification is found among non-European immigrants.

Nevertheless, the official total of 93,000 understates the true scale of the issue as SSB does not count foreign workers who have lived in Norway for less than two years. If new arrivals were included, many of whom take any job at first, the total would be much higher.

In short, the 93,000 figure represents merely a baseline rather than the full scale of the issue.

READ ALSO: Foreigners in Norway face '60 percent' lower chance of promotion

While the proportion of overqualified foreign workers has remained stable at around 40 percent over the past decade, the total number of people affected has gone up significantly.

As overall immigration has increased, the total count of overqualified foreign professionals rose from 73,000 in 2021 to 93,000 in 2025.

From 2022 to 2025, the number of overqualified foreign workers grew by 23 percent, which is a bit faster than the 20 percent growth in the total foreign workforce.

This increase happened mostly because many displaced Ukrainians entered the job market quickly and many of them have higher education degrees but started out in entry-level jobs.

While national economic reports frequently highlight rising average wages and strong purchasing power in Norway, many foreign workers feel these numbers do not match their reality.

Overqualified foreign workers had a median monthly wage of 43,840 kroner, while those in jobs that matched their qualifications earned 66,150 kroner.  This means qualified foreign talent loses over 22,000 kroner every month, adding up to more than 267,000 kroner lost per year!

However, the data reveals another systemic disparity that international residents face in Norway.

Overqualified foreign workers also earn less than overqualified workers in the general population. The median monthly salary for all overqualified workers was 49,340 kroner, which is 12.5 percent more than what overqualified foreign workers make.

Foreign professionals who manage to secure relevant positions earn a 51 percent salary premium over their overqualified peers.

In the case of Ukranians in Norway, the reality is even harsher. In 2025, overqualified immigrants with a Ukrainian background had a median monthly salary of  39,210 kroner (around 26,000 kroner less each month).

Most overqualified workers get jobs in sectors that require less education and have more flexible hiring processes.

In 2025, about 31,000 overqualified immigrants worked in retail, hospitality and catering. Areas where jobs with lower wage levels are more frequent.

Approximately 21,000 overqualified immigrants worked in the health and social care industries.

On the bright side, in the Manufacturing, Construction and Energy sector, overqualification rates have steadily dropped since 2018.  Driven by Norway's growing need for technical experts, foreign engineers and specialists now find it easier to get jobs that match their qualifications.

READ MORE: Which industries employ the most workers in Norway?

Besides the financial loss, this situation is emotionally hard for foreign professionals.

Moving to Norway often means taking a big step back in their careers, losing the professional identity they worked so hard to build. Starting over and taking entry-level jobs just to get by causes frustration, anxiety and stress.

Losing professional status so quickly can also hurt self-esteem and often leads to mental health challenges in the first years after moving.

For former lawyers, architects, or teachers, working as cleaners or waiters is a tough psychological blow. It makes adjusting to a new country even harder, and many in this situation quietly wonder: What am I actually doing in Norway?

READ ALSO: What should you do if your boss or landlord in Norway is exploiting you?

On paper, employment rates among immigrants may have improved. However, this reliance on quick job placement also hides deeper economic vulnerabilities.

Many studies show that not deploying talent already in the country can be costly for national productivity and society as a whole.

Holding 93,000 academics, engineers, educators and specialists in low-skilled roles represents a major economic loss in unutilised human capital. This is especially true now, as Norwegian industries urgently need more qualified workers.

articles.title: Italia forlenger grensekontrollen mot Spania
articles.content:
Italia forlenger den midlertidige opphevelsen av EUs grensefrie avtale med Spania i ytterligere 15 dager.

Det opplyste innenriksdepartementet i Roma onsdag, melder Reuters.

Beslutningen ble tatt på grunn av «den nåværende situasjonen i den spanske eksklaven Ceuta, og spesielt fordi de kritiske forholdene som allerede er identifisert, vedvarer», sa departementet.

Italia suspenderte først Schengen-avtalen med Madrid den 31. juli, som følge av en massestrøm av migranter til Ceuta fra nabolandet Marokko.

Migranter i Europa

Europeiske land krever strengere grensekontroll mot massemigrasjon. På få dager krysset over 70.000 marokkanere ulovlig inn i den spanske eksklaven Ceuta. De fleste er returnert, men minst 100 personer mistet livet.

articles.title: From boning to fokk: The Norwegian words that will shock English speakers
articles.content:
Add The Local as a preferred source
    
                        
                                        
                        Moving to a new country always comes with a learning curve, but for English speakers in Norway, the local language can lead to some truly surprising and hilarious moments, as Irene Andrade explains.

Due to a mix of shared Germanic roots and, in other cases, some funny coincidences, several entirely innocent Norwegian words and traditional names can sound rude, strange, bizarre or even inappropriate to foreigners.

While learning Norwegian and trying to meet the locals, I’ve had plenty of laughs over these awkward moments (though they make for great anecdotes later).

In the world of driving and transportation, Norwegian vocabulary is an absolute minefield for English speakers.

This coincidence gave birth to one of the most famous memes in Norwegian history.

During an international interview, the legendary Norwegian rally driver Petter Solberg tried to explain a racing accident by translating literally: "It’s not the fart that kills, it’s the smell."

What he actually meant to say in Norwegian was, "It's not the speed that kills, it's the crash" (Det er ikke farten som dreper, det er smellet).

Instead, he delivered a timeless joke that has even inspired comedy sketches on NRK, Norway’s national TV channel.

Una publicación compartida de Unlock Norway (Gabriella Mikiewicz) (@unlocknorway)

If a Norwegian tells you they spent the whole Sunday "boning", do not panic. They were simply polishing or waxing their floors (å bone gulvet).

However, they should be careful with their spelling and context when using the expression in an office setting (especially at a state agency in Norway), as shown in this (possibily fake) photo shared with The Local. We probably do not need to explain why context matters so much here.

This word can trip up English speakers in two ways. In winter, it means drifting or blowing snow. When storms hit Norway, meteorologists often warn about heavy fokk in the mountains (the usual term is snøfokk).

At sea, en fokk is a foresail on a sailboat, with types like stormfokk (storm jib) or rullefokk (roller jib).

This means dirt or rubbish. It’s also a mild swear word, like "crap", and you’ll hear it in the phrase wishing fishermen good luck: Skitt fiske!

The tricky part is the pronunciation. In most Norwegian dialects, when "sk" comes before an "i", it sounds just like the English word "shit".

This word means a dot, but it’s also used for a penalty point on your driving licence.

Telling an English speaker you got a prikk from the police will definitely require some immediate context.

This word translates to boiling or cooking; however, for some English speakers, reading it can instantly cause a double-take.

It also happens to be the name of one of Norway’s most famous floating saunas (KOK), which can lead to some funny misunderstandings. Asking your British or American friend to "spend a warm afternoon inside the hot KOK" might not be the best icebreaker.

In Norwegian, ass is a very common slang abbreviation for the word altså (which can have several meanings, including "though").

Used at the end of a sentence for emphasis, it can also be a way of sounding cool and more modern, meaning "dude" or "man".

For example, "Det var en kul fest, ass" translates to "That was a cool party, man". However, when Norwegians casually carry this over into English conversations, sentences like "She was great, ass" can leave foreigners a bit confused.

Some of Norway’s oldest and most respected names can get lots of laughs abroad. If you already live in Norway and have met a few locals, you have almost certainly had that awkward moment of thinking, "Sorry, could you repeat that?"

It is an ancient male name derived from the Old Norse word for the "point of an arrow or sword." Unfortunately, introducing yourself in London or New York with "Hi, I'm Odd" usually leaves people wondering what’s so strange about you.

Fun fact, 15,904 men have Odd as part of their first name in Norway. I checked.

Then we have the opposite side of the coin with the name Even.

While perfectly normal in Norway, the absolute peak of this phonetic coincidence was shared by a Reddit user who confirmed: "My neighbour's name is literally Odd Even..."

This is the Norwegian variant of the classic name Simon.

It’s a common and respected name across Scandinavia, with 8,652 men named Simen in Norway.

However, because it shares its exact pronunciation with the male biological term in English, international business introductions can lead to some highly uncomfortable situations.

As one Reddit user shared: "I laughed so much when I met my first Simen in Norway. I was like wtf, why doesn't anyone else notice it?!"

Those were the names that first caught my eye, but then I stumbled upon a question online that I just couldn't ignore: “Wondering if there are any Bent Christians out there?”

I couldn't leave it at that. And well, I'm so glad I looked it up. There are exactly 12 men in Norway whose only first name is indeed Bent Christian.

Are we forgetting any? Have you had a "WTF" moment while living or travelling in Norway? Let us know in the comments and (pretty please!) share your photos.

articles.title: Sigrid-drapsmann vil løslates
articles.content:
Mannen (51) fra Sunnmøre, som ble dømt til tvungent psykisk helsevern for drapet på Sigrid Giskegjerde Schjetne i 2013, begjærer seg løslatt. Det skriver Dagbladet.

27. oktober skal mannen møte i Sunnmøre tingrett for å få vurdert om dommen på tvungent psykisk helsevern skal forlenges i tre nye år.

Mannens forsvarer, Ida Andenæs Mehren, bekrefter overfor Dagbladet at han nå for første gang vil begjære seg løslatt.

Statsadvokat Ingvild Thorn Nordheim sier til avisen at det er en ordinær forlengelsessak som skal vurderes av domstolen.

Påtalemyndigheten mener at han ikke bør løslates på grunn av gjentakelsesfare.

Drapet på Sigrid Schjetne

I juni 2016, fire år etter drapet, har den siktede 41-åringen tilstått drapet på den 16-årige Oslo-jenta Sigrid Giskegjerde Schjetne, ifølge Dagbladet. Da saken var oppe i Borgarting lagmannsrett ble mannen dømt til tvungent psykisk helsevern.

Drapet på Sigrid Giskegjerde Schjetne

Sigrid Giskegjerde Schjetne (16) forsvant på Østensjø i Oslo natt til søndag 5. august 2012. Mandag 3. september 2012 pågrep politiet i Follo to personer i et verksted på Kolbotn. Senere samme kveld ble den savnede funnet død i et skogholt i nærheten av verkstedet på Kolbotn. En 64-åring ble løslatt torsdag 1. november 2012, og saken mot ham ble henlagt. Samtidig tok Riksadvokaten ut tiltale mot en 38-åring. 25. oktober 2013 ble 38-åringen dømt til tvungent psykisk helsevern for drapet på Sigrid Giskegjerde Schjetne. 38-åringen anket på stedet. 22. april starter ankesaken i Borgarting lagmannsrett.

articles.title: Brende: Møtte ikkje Epstein då han var utanriksminister
articles.content:
Han er den einaste av dei som møter i høyringane i dag, som ein veit har hatt kontakt med og møtte den dømte seksualforbryteren Jeffrey Epstein. Det skjedde i åra 2018 og 2019, åra etter han gjekk av som utanriksminister.

Han startar å svare at han aldri hadde kontakt med Epstein då han var utanriksminister.

Kontakten skjedde då han var president i World Economic Forum.

Først nekta han for å ha hatt kontakt med Epstein, og det angra han på i dag.

– Eg vil beklage at eg ikkje var ærleg med ein gong, seier Brende.

– Eg var nok redd for at kontakten ville bli tolka som noko meir enn den var. Og for at det ville ramme forumet rett før Davos. Det viste eg dårleg handlekraft, seier Brende.

Jeffrey Epstein-saken

Onsdag og tordag skal flere tidligere statsråder svare i en høring på Stortinget. De flere millionene Epstein-dokumentene som USAs justisdepartement offentliggjorde tidligere i år, har fått konsekvenser også langt inn i det offentlige Norge.

articles.title: Streiken i private barnehager er avblåst
articles.content:
Partene i PBL-oppgjøret har kommet til enighet kort tid før meklingsfristen. Dermed blir det ingen streik i den private barnehagesektoren.

– Vi har blitt enige med PBL om et oppgjør som sikrer våre medlemmer reallønnsvekst og økt lønnsutvikling, bekrefter forhandlingsleder i Fagforbundet Line Tollefsen overfor NRK.

Oppgjøret innebærer også at pensjonsordningen holdes på dagens nivå, sier nestleder i Delta Marit Solheim.

– Det har aldri vært et alternativ for oss å svekke nivået på pensjonsordningen, og vi er godt fornøyd med at vi har klart å beholde dagens pensjonsnivå.

Rundt 70 private barnehager i 12 kommuner ville blitt rammet av streik dersom partene ikke hadde kommet til enighet.

Administrerende direktør i PBL Jørn-Tommy Schjelderup beskriver meklingen som utfordrende.

articles.title: Today in Norway: A roundup of the latest news on Tuesday
articles.content:
Add The Local as a preferred source
    
                        
                                        
                        Diesel prices hit record high above 31 kroner per litre, unusually warm weather across Norway, Epstein hearing begins on Wednesday, and more news on Tuesday.

Diesel prices hit record high above 31 kroner per litre

Drivers in many areas across the country are seeing record-high fuel prices, with diesel now costing more than 31 kroner per litre, as reported by newspaper VG.

Prices hit a new record after temporary tax cuts ended on September 1st.

One local driver told VG: "The prices are high. When I saw that it was over 30 kroner today, I thought: Where will this stop?"

READ MORE: How and where to get the cheapest fuel in Norway

Epstein hearing begins on Wednesday in the Norwegian parliament

A historic two-day hearing in parliament starts on Wednesday to investigate possible corrupt links between Norway’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the late American Jeffrey Epstein.

Eleven current and former foreign and development ministers will be questioned by the parliamentary oversight committee as reported by broadcaster TV 2.

Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre, who was Minister of Foreign Affairs from 2005 to 2012, will appear on the first day of the hearing.

Former Foreign Ministers Børge Brende and Ine Eriksen Søreide will also attend the hearing on the first day.

Foreign Minister Espen Barth Eide and former Foreign Minister Anniken Huitfeldt will appear on the second day on October 1st.

The head of the control committee, Per-Willy Amundsen (from the Progress Party Frp), said expectations must be realistic.

“We do not think we can cover everything in just two days, because the cases are so complex. It goes back to the Oslo process in the early 1990s and involves many people,” Amundsen told news agency NTB.

Record funding to help Norwegian kindergarten staff

The government has announced in an official statement that it will provide 112 million kroner to help more than 1,900 current kindergarten assistants take a teacher training course this autumn.

Each employee will receive 60,000 kroner to cover costs like substitute staff, travel, or study materials. The goal is to help solve staffing shortages in early education.

“There is a great need for more kindergarten teachers. That is why we have strengthened one of our most effective measures: giving more people who already work in kindergartens the opportunity to train as kindergarten teachers while continuing to work. This is a very popular offer where the vast majority both complete their education and remain in the profession,” said Minister of Education Kari Nessa Nordtun.

For parents with children in barnehage, or those planning a family in Norway, having more qualified staff should improve education quality.

For international residents, working as a kindergarten assistant is a common entry-level job in Norway. This government programme gives those already in the sector a fully funded way to gain formal Norwegian qualifications, increase their earning potential,  and also build a long-term career.

Norwegian vocabulary: å utdanne - to undergo education or training for a profession

​Man sentenced to prison for calling police officer 'fucking foreigner'

A man in his 20 has been sentenced to 26 days in prison without parole by the Frostating Court of Appeal after calling a police officer in Ålesund a "fucking foreigner", as reported by media outlet Aftenposten.

The appeal court unanimously ruled that the remark was intentional, derogatory, harassing, and racist.

The 26-day sentence also includes charges of violence against the police, assaulting a public official, and refusing to identify himself during the incident. The man pleaded not guilty.

Norwegian vocabulary: jævla utlending -  it is a derogatory slur meaning fucking foreigner.

Unusually warm weather expected across Norway this week

Parts of Western and Northern Norway will see unusually high temperatures this week, due to a warm wind coming from southern Europe.

"When the wind passes over mountains, waves form in the airflow. In some places, the air is pushed down into the lowlands, causing temperatures to rise. This is known as the Foehn effect," weather experts at Yr explained.

Temperatures in Western Norway could reach up to 25C, while Trøndelag and Nordland are also expected to see temperatures above 20C. This brings a surprisingly summery end to September.

"The northern part of Vestland and Møre og Romsdal has the greatest potential for 25C," Patrick Stoll, duty meteorologist at the Meteorological Institute, told newspaper VG.

Norwegian vocabulary: føneffekten - the Foehn effect

articles.title: How to prepare for Norway's citizenship and social studies exams
articles.content:
Add The Local as a preferred source
    
                        
                                        
                        One of the requirements to become a citizen in Norway is to pass either the social studies or the citizenship test. The Local has put together some advice on how to best prepare.

The process of acquiring Norwegian citizenship takes years, thanks to the residence requirements, and other conditions such as the language exams, background check, citizenship, or social studies test mean it's a far from straightforward road.

Still, it should be worth it in the end, even if you have to wait a lengthy time to receive a decision on your application due to long processing times.

The main difference between which test you may take will depend on the type of residence you were granted when you first moved to Norway.

The state offers an introduction to Norway programme to some people who move to Norway. This course, usually provided along with language training, aims to get new arrivals up to speed with the country.

Those typically offered these courses originally arrived in Norway on a family immigration or asylum seeker permit.

If you arrived in Norway under the EEA or work permit rules, then you will not have been offered this course.

For those who have done this introductory course, you will likely have been presented with the opportunity to sit the social studies exam. If you have sat and passed this exam in Norwegian, then you are all set, as the exam doesn't have an expiration date and can be submitted with the rest of your documents.

Even if you didn't get the chance to sit this exam in Norwegian or complete the course, fret not, the syllabus for the course will be the same as for the citizenship exam. Therefore, you should have picked up a few things that will be useful for the test.

Most applicants who didn't do the social studies course will probably prefer the citizenship test as it is slightly easier.

The reason it's easier isn't the content of the test itself, as both tests are drawn from the same syllabus. Instead, the language used in the citizenship test is considered more accessible.

Both tests require knowledge of Norwegian history, the school system, healthcare, politics, and geography. They also include questions on societal norms in Norway, working life, and government agencies.

The syllabus is available online and can be divided into the topics of "education skills and the labour market," "family, health and daily life," and "Norway now and before."

These different topics are broken down into various sub-topics. These topics will cover how a system works in Norway and the cultural values behind a particular system – understanding both will give you the tools you need to ace either exam.

Course materials are available in several languages (however, the online portal can be glitchy). The curriculum is found on the website of HK-dir (The Norwegian Directorate for Higher Education and Skills).

Thankfully, having the curriculum available should help.

Another helpful aspect of the online curriculum is that it includes discussion points and multiple-choice questions.

For the discussion points, ask somebody to read out the questions to you in English or Norwegian as another way of testing your retention.

There is also an official mock available online. The only downside is that the questions don't change. Still, it should be good for familiarising yourself with how your knowledge will be tested and learning the language used for the test.

There are also unofficial practise exams online. Some of these charge users for access to example questions. Still, there are free mocks available online that applicants can take.

With the right preparation, you should be able to sit the test when you feel ready rather than rushing into it. Local municipalities are responsible for providing the exams and there are quite a few opportunities to take the test throughout the year.

If you need more time to get up to speed with your Norwegian reading skills, or the syllabus then its better to wait a few weeks or couple of months for more slots to open up.

Alternatively, if you want everything ready to submit when you meet the residence requirements, and your Norwegian skills are good enough, then you can take the test ahead of time.

Either way, there's no point in booking a police appointment to hand your documents in until you've passed the test – so there shouldn't be any need to put yourself under any pressure.

articles.title: Tiltalt for frihetsberøvelse av 12-åring
articles.content:
En mann i 40-årene er tiltalt for frihetsberøvelse etter å ha holdt en 12-åring som lekte «ring på og stikk» sperret inne i fjor høst.

Ifølge politiet holdt mannen barnet fast inntil en vegg før han dro henne med seg inn inn i huset og ned i kjelleren. Mannen skal også ha uttalt «du vet at du ikke kommer hjem i natt» til jenta, skriver Avisa Oslo.

Hun ble sluppet ut etter drøyt 15 minutter, da en nabo ringte på døra.

Mannen er også tiltalt for kroppskrenkelse etter å ha løpt etter, holdt fast og dratt i et annet barn som hadde ringt på døra hans rundt en måned tidligere.

Rettssaken skal gå i Oslo tingrett i desember. Det er ikke kjent hvordan mannen stiller seg til anklagene, ifølge avisa.

Oslo politidistrikt

Oslo politidistrikt omfatter kommunene Oslo, Asker og Bærum. Politimester i Oslo siden mai 2023 er Ida Melbo Øystese.

Saker i Oslo tingrett

Oslo tingrett er Norges største tingrett og behandler straffesaker, sivile saker og forvaltningssaker. Tingretten holder til i Oslo tinghus, midt i Oslo sentrum.

articles.content:

De mener undervannsdronen drev spionasjevirksomhet i det strategisk viktige stredet. Dronen blir nå undersøkt av IRGCs spesialister, opplyses det.
